title: Minimum Amount of Damage Dealt to Bob
statement:
Bob fights `n` enemies. Enemy `i` starts with `health[i]` health and, as long as its health is above 0, hurts Bob by `damage[i]` points every second. Each second happens in this order:

1. Every enemy that is still alive deals its damage to Bob.
2. Bob picks one living enemy and lowers its health by `power`. An enemy whose health reaches 0 or less is dead and deals no more damage.

Bob may pick any living enemy each second. Return the minimum total damage Bob can receive before all `n` enemies are dead.
signature: long minDamage(int power, int[] damage, int[] health)
notes:
## Intuition

Enemy `i` needs `time[i] = ceil(health[i] / power)` hits, and it hurts Bob in every second up to and including the one in which it dies. Splitting hits between enemies only delays someone's death. So Bob picks an order, and an enemy finishing at second `elapsed` costs `damage[i] * elapsed`.

Which order? Compare two neighbours `a` and `b` in the queue. Swapping them affects nobody else. Killing `a` first makes `b` wait `time[a]` extra seconds, costing `damage[b] * time[a]`; the other way costs `damage[a] * time[b]`. So `a` goes first when `time[a] * damage[b] < time[b] * damage[a]`, meaning a smaller `time / damage` ratio. Sorting by that rule gives an order no swap can improve. (The brute force instead searches every possible attack sequence.)

## Approach

1. Compute `time[i]`, the hits enemy `i` needs.
2. Sort the indices in `order` with the cross-multiplied comparison `time[a] * damage[b] - time[b] * damage[a]`.
3. Walk `order`, adding each enemy's `time` to `elapsed`, the second it dies.
4. That enemy hurt Bob in each of those `elapsed` seconds: add `damage[i] * elapsed` to `total`.

## Example 1, step by step

`power = 4` gives `time = [1, 2, 2, 2]`. The ratios `time / damage` are 1, 1, 0.67 and 0.5, so the order is 3, 2, then 0 and 1, which tie (either order costs the same). Enemy 3 dies at second 2 (`4 * 2 = 8`), enemy 2 at 4 (`3 * 4 = 12`), enemy 0 at 5 (`1 * 5 = 5`) and enemy 1 at 7 (`2 * 7 = 14`). The total is 39.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n) for the sort; the rest is linear.
- Space: O(n) for `time` and `order`.

## Pitfalls

- Sorting by damage alone fails: with `power = 1`, `damage = [3, 2]`, `health = [6, 1]` killing the big hitter first costs 32, but the quick kill first costs 23.
- Sorting by time alone fails too: with `power = 1`, `damage = [1, 10]`, `health = [1, 3]` it costs 41 instead of 34.
- Use hits needed, `ceil(health / power)`, not raw health, and compare products rather than divided ratios to stay exact.
- The total can pass 2^31; Java and C need a 64-bit result.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `time` | `time[i]`: seconds of attacks enemy `i` needs |
| `order` | enemy indices in the order Bob kills them |
| `i` | the enemy being killed |
| `elapsed` | the second in which that enemy dies |
| `total` | damage Bob has taken from the enemies handled so far |

narration.2: Each enemy needs ceil(health / power) seconds of attacks to die.
narration.3: List the enemy indices so they can be put in kill order.
narration.4: Kill a before b when time[a] / damage[a] is smaller, compared by cross-multiplying to stay exact.
narration.5: elapsed will be the second in which the current enemy dies.
narration.6: total adds up all damage Bob receives.
narration.7: Kill the enemies one after another in the sorted order.
narration.8: Bob spends time[i] more seconds on this enemy, so it dies at second elapsed.
narration.9: This enemy hurt Bob in every second until then: damage[i] each second for elapsed seconds.
narration.11: The sum over all enemies is the minimum total damage.
